title: Two projects. Different questions.
description: Compare ArtiSense sensing research with AIFIELD photonic design and simulation: intended users, outputs, evidence and the next validation questions.
lead: ArtiSense explores how light could reveal chemical information. AIFIELD explores how engineers can design and analyze the photonic systems behind it.

sections.title: ArtiSense
paragraphs: The question: can a miniaturized photonic system detect a useful chemical signal and interpret it reliably? The intended users and form factors depend on a measurement task that still needs validation.

Available work concerns optical feasibility and chip design, including glucose-related research. The next evidence needed is a controlled physical comparison that separates the target response from other influences.
rows: Extract useful chemical information from an optical response.
Research toward non-invasive sensing; wearable form is an ambition.
Proposed architecture and design/simulation work, not a validated medical product.

sections.title: AIFIELD
paragraphs: The question: how can an engineer move from geometry and process assumptions to interpretable photonic simulations? AIFIELD is aimed at people designing and assessing optical systems.

The September 2026 snapshot describes design, classical solvers and partial agent assistance. Neural optical-field prediction has its own research constraints. Reproducible comparisons and clear input conditions are the next useful basis for evaluation.
rows: Connect layout choices with model-based analysis.
Photonic designers and engineers evaluating simulation workflows.
Designs and simulated results; neural field prediction remains research.

sections.title: One example connects the work. Evidence keeps it distinct.
paragraphs: The photonic glucose chip-design example links AIFIELD’s engineering workflow to the sensing objective associated with ArtiSense. The design activity belongs to AIFIELD; the question of what can actually be measured belongs to ArtiSense.
A useful simulation can guide the next experiment. It cannot, by itself, validate a sensor, demonstrate clinical accuracy or establish a commercial relationship.
